issues.legal_issue: A resident personally affected by alleged unlawful activity that harms a wider group may maintain a public-interest writ proceeding.
material_facts: The appellant lived in the building where the diagnostic centre operated and was personally affected by its operation.
Residents made repeated complaints about nuisance, hardship, traffic and parking problems caused by the centre.
The challenge alleged violations of land-use requirements and harm to local residents, rather than only a private dispute.
issues.conclusion: The proceeding raised matters of public interest, and the appellant had standing to pursue it; the High Court’s contrary finding was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, standing is not confined to a person asserting an individual proprietary right where a legal wrong affects a determinate group. Public-interest standing is to be applied liberally to facilitate access to justice. The Court relied on S. P. Gupta v. President of India, State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal, Gadde Venkateswara Rao v. State of A.P., and the standing principles discussed in Calcutta Gas Company (Proprietary) Ltd. v. State of West Bengal.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_proceeding and group_harm_alleged and multiple_residents_complained and petitioner_personally_affected

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A person brought a constitutional writ proceeding challenging alleged unlawful activity.
predicates.group_harm_alleged: The proceeding alleged that the activity caused legal harm or nuisance to a group of residents, rather than only a private injury.
predicates.multiple_residents_complained: More than one resident complained to public authorities about the activity.
predicates.petitioner_personally_affected: The person bringing the proceeding was also personally affected by the activity.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ proceeding alleges harm to a group, multiple residents have complained, and the petitioner is personally affected, the proceeding is maintainable as a public-interest writ.

issues.legal_issue: A regularisation certificate cannot authorize commercial activity in a residential property when the applicable mixed-use requirements are unmet or the certificate purports to authorize the activity retrospectively.
material_facts: The certificate authorized a pathological laboratory in a residential property but described conditions concerning a nursing home.
The laboratory operated in the basement, ground floor, mezzanine floor and first floor, although the certificate identified only the ground and first floors.
The property had multiple dwelling units, and the laboratory’s owners did not reside there.
No traffic or environmental assessment required under the then-applicable mixed-use rules was produced.

The applicable rules restricted activity in the relevant residential categories and imposed limits on the floors, extent and conditions of mixed use; the record also did not establish payment of charges for basement use exceeding permissible floor area.
The certificate purported to regularise activity under a plan that was not yet in force when the certificate was issued, and the operation also contravened the applicable earlier plan.
issues.conclusion: The certificate was impermissible and unsustainable in law and was quashed.
issues.legal_principle: The Delhi Master Plan 2001 permitted mixed use only after the required traffic and environmental assessment and subject to limits on location, extent and who could operate the activity; it also excluded nursing homes. The Master Plan 2021 permitted specified public and semi-public activities only subject to its general and additional conditions, including restrictions applicable to residential categories, the rule allowing only one mixed-use activity in a dwelling unit, and limits on basement use and floor-area charges. The Court held that a later plan could not retrospectively validate the certificate and relied on Priyanka Estate International (P) Ltd. v. State of Assam for the principle that unauthorised construction or use cannot be legitimised at the expense of the public interest.

rule.if: land_use_authorization_challenge and residential_property and (mixed_use_requirements_unmet or certificate_activity_mismatch or certificate_retroactively_applied)

predicates.land_use_authorization_challenge: A proceeding challenged official authorization for non-residential activity in a residential property.
predicates.residential_property: The activity took place in property used as a residence.
predicates.mixed_use_requirements_unmet: The activity or its extent did not satisfy applicable safeguards governing mixed use, including relevant limits on location, extent, occupancy, assessment or floor-area use.
predicates.certificate_activity_mismatch: The certificate identified one kind of activity while its conditions described a materially different kind of activity.
predicates.certificate_retroactively_applied: The certificate purported to authorize activity from a time before the legal basis relied on for that authorization was in force.

issues.definition: A challenged authorization for non-residential activity in a residence is invalid when applicable mixed-use requirements are unmet, the certificate describes a different activity, or it purports to operate retrospectively.

issues.legal_issue: An establishment that causes prohibited pollution and operates without required prior consent cannot lawfully continue its activity.
material_facts: The pollution-control authority’s report recorded chemical substances and pollution associated with the laboratory’s operation.

The laboratory used heavy equipment, diesel generators, air conditioners and other materials, and the record described air and noise pollution, effects on residents, and chemical discharge affecting water.
The owners had not obtained the required prior consent for an operation likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent.
The generators were placed in the setback area, and the Court found the structure to be contrary to building requirements.
The Court found that the activity violated the applicable land-use restrictions on hazardous, polluting or incompatible processes.
issues.conclusion: The laboratory’s operation was unlawful, and the owners were directed to close it and shift it to alternative premises; the municipal authority was directed to close or seal the activities if the owners did not comply.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the prohibition in clause 15.5 of the Master Plan 2021 on specified hazardous, incompatible or polluting activity, and the prior-consent requirement in section 25 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act as cited in the judgment. It also relied on the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, section 2(e) of that Act defining a hazardous substance, and Article 21. Under Noise Pollution (V) in Re, noise reaching unpleasant or obnoxious levels may violate the right to a peaceful and pollution-free life; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India recognizes the public authorities’ and citizens’ obligations concerning a hygienic environment.

rule.if: challenge_to_polluting_activity and hazardous_or_polluting_process and required_prior_pollution_consent_absent and environmental_harm_to_residents

predicates.challenge_to_polluting_activity: A proceeding challenged the operation of an establishment alleged to cause pollution.
predicates.hazardous_or_polluting_process: The establishment used or emitted substances or processes associated with hazardous, incompatible or polluting effects.
predicates.required_prior_pollution_consent_absent: The operator had not obtained prior consent required for an operation likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent.
predicates.environmental_harm_to_residents: The operation caused or threatened air, water or noise pollution affecting residents or public health.

issues.definition: When a challenged establishment uses a hazardous or polluting process, lacks required prior pollution consent, and harms or threatens residents, it must cease operation.

issues.legal_issue: Public authorities must take enforcement action when they receive repeated complaints about unlawful activity and instead allow it to continue or regularise it despite violations.
material_facts: Residents repeatedly complained to the municipal and pollution-control authorities about the laboratory’s operation and its effects.
The authorities did not take prompt action to stop the activity despite notices and complaints.
The municipal authority issued a certificate purporting to regularise the activity, which the Court found impermissible.
The Court found that the authorities had failed to discharge their statutory duties and directed them to ensure that the unlawful activity stopped.
issues.conclusion: The municipal and pollution-control authorities were directed to ensure that the unlawful activity stopped and to take prompt steps to close or seal the premises if the owners did not comply with the closure direction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that statutory authorities must discharge their duties to enforce land-use and environmental requirements and cannot justify inaction by relying on an impermissible regularisation certificate. It relied on the statutory framework discussed in the judgment, including the Delhi Development Act and environmental laws, and on M.C. Mehta v. Union of India concerning public authorities’ duties to protect the environment and public health.

rule.if: public_law_enforcement_proceeding and repeated_complaints_to_authorities and authorities_failed_to_act and authorities_allowed_activity_to_continue_despite_violations

predicates.public_law_enforcement_proceeding: A proceeding sought enforcement of legal requirements governing activity that affects the public.
predicates.repeated_complaints_to_authorities: Residents repeatedly reported the activity and its effects to the responsible public authorities.
predicates.authorities_failed_to_act: The responsible authorities did not take prompt steps to address the reported activity.
predicates.authorities_allowed_activity_to_continue: The activity continued despite violations, including because an authority purported to regularise it.

issues.definition: In a public-law enforcement proceeding, repeated complaints, official inaction and continued activity despite violations require the authorities to take enforcement action.
